item.title: Inflation anxiety drags on AI stocks for a second day as markets point to a mixed open
item.description: Global shares mostly declined, led by sharp drops in Asia, as a sell-off of technology shares deepened after U.S. stocks fell on hotter-than-expected inflation data.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: Tech stocks appeared to be headed for another sell-off before the bell with inflation anxiety hammering that high-growth sector ahead of the U.S. earnings season. Futures for the S&P 500 fell 0.2% before the opening bell, while futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3%. Nasdaq futures tumbled 1%. Artificial intelligence stocks were down again after taking a beating a day earlier. CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, fell another 3.8% early after tumbling 15.5% a day earlier, its worst day since February. GE Vernova, which is hoping to electrify power-hungry data centers, dropped 3.2% after a 6.2% decline on Wednesday and Oracle sank 1.6%, adding to its nearly 9% loss in the previous session. Chipmaker and AI darling Nvidia fell 1.6% in early trading, as did Broadcom, while Advanced Micro Devices retreated 3.1%. The yield on 10-year bonds eased to 5.09% from 5.32%, but remains elevated. Higher bond yields that have made borrowing more expensive could make it more difficult for companies to raise cash to build data centers and fill them with AI chips. The latest inflation figures showed Wednesday that prices remain well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target, putting in play another potential interest rate hike before the end of the year, which also puts pressure on the equities market. The government’s latest report on wholesale prices, the producer price index, arrives Thursday along with another trove of corporate earnings reports. In Asia, South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index lost 7.6% to 5,554.22. It plummeted more than 16% over the past month and was well below the 9,000 mark that it crossed in June at its all-time high driven by optimism over the global artificial intelligence frenzy. Samsung Electronics slid 9.5% and South Korean memory chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 11.1%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 tumbled 4.9% to 64,425.95. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group lost 9.3%. Chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron dropped 7.8%, and memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings lost 12.3%. Taiwan’s Taiex, which also benefited from the AI boom, fell 3.4%. Its leading chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, dropped 2% ahead of its earnings report. TSMC reported on Thursday another record profit for the latest quarter, which was better than what analysts had expected, and the company said AI demand remains very strong. “The problem for heavily technology-weighted markets such as Korea and Taiwan, to a lesser extent Japan, is that any risk to perceived AI spending growth may lead to slower demand growth for chips and equipment,” said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research for Asia at Morningstar. “The key issue is a possible mismatch between the market’s growth expectations for the tech sector and what may eventuate,” she said. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1% to 24,062.72. The Shanghai Composite index slipped 1.6% to 3,707.48. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 edged down 0.1% to 8,719.70. At midday in Europe, Britain’s FTSE 100 rose 0.7%, France’s CAC 40 gave back 0.3% and Germany’s DAX was down 0.4%. Oil prices fell as tensions and uncertainties surrounding global oil supply and the situation in the Middle East dragged on. Brent crude, the international standard, declined more than 1% to $104.91 per barrel. That’s still elevated compared with the approximately $72 per barrel level before the start of the Iran war in late February. U.S. crude was up 23 cents a barrel to $95.32. By Chan Ho-him and Matt Ott

item.title: CoreWeave shares, bonds slide further as AI debt fears mount
item.description: AI cloud firm CoreWeave’s shares and bonds slumped further on Thursday despite CEO assurances about its strong deal backlog, in one of the deepest crises of investor confidence yet in an AI build-out ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: AI cloud firm CoreWeave’s shares and bonds slumped further on Thursday despite CEO assurances about its strong deal backlog, in one of the deepest crises of investor confidence yet in an AI build-out increasingly fueled by borrowing. The company’s stock fell six per cent in premarket trading after a more than 15 per cent drop on Wednesday, among the biggest decliners in a global tech stocks rout. The yield on its April-issued bonds due 2031 surged past 16 per cent, above the level that typically signals distress, drawing a “yikes” from Elon Musk on social media. Loss-making CoreWeave, which has around US$50 billion in debt, has in recent days become the focus of growing doubts about whether the tech industry can sustain a data center boom that is saddling newer cloud firms with heavy borrowing and straining cash flow even at giants such as Google-owner Alphabet. The cost of insuring the Nvidia-backed company’s debt against default has climbed to around 1,000 basis points, a level that implies a nearly 63 per cent chance the company defaults within five years, up from about 30 per cent a year ago. CoreWeave leads a group of newer cloud providers known as neoclouds, which rent out computing power from tight in supply and costly Nvidia processors to meet the tech industry’s soaring demand, often leaning on borrowing to fund the chip purchases. Critics say that leaves such firms exposed to any cooling in AI demand, while the chips lose value as newer generations arrive, forcing another round of heavy spending to replace them. CoreWeave, which in August raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion to between $35 billion and $39 billion, is expected to post revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion, according to analysts’ estimates. Growing worries about the build-out, on which U.S. tech giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year, have in recent days rippled through the stocks that have been the market’s biggest winners since ChatGPT’s November 2022 launch. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a closely watched gauge of semiconductor stocks, has erased over $1.6 trillion in market value in an 11.6 per cent slide over the past six sessions. The tech-heavy Nasdaq has declined more than three per cent in the period. On Thursday, tech shares fell across Asia, Europe and the U.S., dragging broader markets lower on fears that high and rising interest rates could bring a reckoning for the sector. CoreWeave’s neocloud rivals such as Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren fell between 3.2 per cent and five per cent. ‘Unlimited’ pools of capital The CoreWeave sell-off came as its co-founder Brannin McBee told the Financial Times the company was seeking an investment-grade rating that would open the door to “unlimited” capital. On the same day, research firm Gartner said that about 80 per cent of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, and that more than $3.5 trillion of AI infrastructure spending could face impairment if AI providers keep up their current pace of investment. “In 2026, AI providers are expected to spend nearly $1 trillion on AI infrastructure, and are forecast to invest an additional $6 trillion between 2027 and 2030,” said Will Sommer, analyst at Gartner. “However, our research indicates enterprise and consumer AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures during this period.” CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator pushed back on the concerns in an internal memo on Wednesday seen by Reuters, telling employees the company’s deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations and that markets can sometimes “misunderstand and act irrationally.” (Reporting by Aditya Soni, Anhata Rooprai and Shashwat Chauhan in Bengaluru)

item.title: Client satisfaction scores rise slightly among banks, according to J.D. Power survey
item.description: Canadians are slightly upping their customer satisfaction rankings for banks this year, according to a new J.D. Power survey, which says the higher scores are mainly driven by improvements in the Big ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Canadians are slightly upping their customer satisfaction rankings for banks this year, according to a new J.D. Power survey, which says the higher scores are mainly driven by improvements in the Big Five banks. The survey showed that overall customer satisfaction rose by three points on a 1,000-point scale. RBC ranked the highest in terms of customer satisfaction among the Big Five banks for a third consecutive year, with a score of 619. BMO and CIBC were tied for second place, with a score of 611. TD Bank came in fourth with a score of 610. Among midsize banks, Tangerine Bank was ranked the highest for a 15th consecutive year with a score of 676. The survey points to a growing threat of competition, with newer fintechs outperforming Big Five lenders and midsize banks across certain key factors. The survey found 17 per cent of gen Z and gen Y traditional banking customers say they are likely or will definitely switch their primary lender in the next 12 months, which marked the highest level recorded in the past five years. Among younger customers, fees and competitive rates were found to be a vulnerability for larger banks. “Younger customers can be satisfied with their bank and still leave if they see a better opportunity to save money elsewhere,” Paul McAdam, senior director of banking and payments intelligence at JD Power, said in a news release. “When household budgets are tight, a monthly banking fee becomes an expense worth reconsidering. Traditional banks cannot take the next generation’s loyalty for granted.” The use of AI among lenders was seen to be unclear to most customers, with only 12 per cent of traditional retail bank customers indicating they understand how their lender uses AI. Meanwhile, fraud prevention and data security led the list in how customers prefer their bank to use AI. Survey results were taken from responses from 14,038 retail banking customers across large and mid-sized lenders. Responses were taken between January and February as well as from July to August. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026. Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

item.title: The bull market turns four. Is age really just a number?: Stan Wong
item.description: At four years old, the current bull market remains about a year and a half younger than the historical average. Of course, this does not mean another 18 months of gains are assured. Rather, it ...
item.content:encoded:
“I’m still standing (yeah, yeah, yeah).” Elton John’s famous lyric seems particularly fitting as the S&P 500 bull market celebrates its fourth birthday this week.

On Oct. 12, 2022, the S&P 500 closed at 3,577, roughly 25 per cent below its previous peak. Inflation was running at multidecade highs, the Federal Reserve was aggressively raising interest rates, recession forecasts were widespread and investor sentiment was deeply pessimistic. Yet that October low marked the beginning of a new bull market, generally defined as a sustained rise of at least 20 per cent from a previous market low. Since then, the S&P 500 has climbed more than 118 per cent, excluding dividends, overcoming considerable economic uncertainty and several significant corrections. But is this bull market beginning to show its age, or could there still be room to run? Four years old, but not necessarily old Investors often assume that the longer a bull market lasts, the closer it must be to ending. However, market cycles do not follow a predetermined timetable. My analysis of Bloomberg data examined 11 completed S&P 500 bull markets dating back to 1949. The average lasted about 5.5 years, although durations varied considerably. The shortest continued for just 21 months, from 2020 to 2022, while the longest persisted for more than 12 years, from 1987 to 2000. At four years old, the current bull market remains about a year and a half younger than the historical average. Of course, this does not mean another 18 months of gains are assured. Rather, it illustrates why market age alone is a poor indicator of when a bull market might end. While bull market longevity provides useful historical context, an even more interesting question is how stocks have performed after reaching their fourth anniversary. What happens in year five? Of the 11 completed bull markets since 1949, six lasted long enough to complete their fifth year. Further analysis of Bloomberg data showed that all six generated positive S&P 500 price returns during their fifth year, averaging 17.4 per cent. Returns ranged from 4.5 per cent during the bull market that began in 1987 to an impressive 30.4 per cent during the fifth year of the advance that started in 1982. More recently, the bull market that emerged from the global financial crisis gained another 23.3 per cent during its fifth year, eventually continuing until February 2020. While encouraging, these findings reflect a relatively small sample of bull markets that survived five full years. They provide historical perspective rather than a reliable forecast of future returns. The impressive fifth-year gain following the 1982 market bottom, for example, was followed just two months later by the October 1987 stock market crash. History offers perspective, not a timetable. Corrections are part of the journey Even long-running bull markets rarely advance in a straight line. Consider 2025, when the S&P 500 declined nearly 19 per cent on a closing basis between February and April, approaching the conventional 20 per cent threshold that defines a bear market. Yet the broader bull market survived, subsequently recovering and advancing to new highs. Investors who interpreted that correction as the beginning of a prolonged downturn risked missing the recovery. It serves as an important reminder that market volatility and the end of a bull market are not necessarily the same thing. Fundamentals matter more than birthdays Rather than focusing on market age, investors should pay closer attention to corporate earnings, valuations and economic conditions. Artificial intelligence investment continues to support capital spending across industries, but elevated valuations and high expectations leave less room for disappointment. Broader market participation is also important, as a rally supported by more sectors and companies generally provides a healthier foundation than one dependent on a handful of market leaders. Meanwhile, rising oil prices could reignite inflationary pressures, complicating monetary policy and keeping bond yields elevated. Ultimately, corporate profitability, valuations, interest rates and investor expectations will determine whether the bull market continues, not how many birthdays it has celebrated. Investing beyond the birthday Selling simply because a bull market has lasted longer than expected can be costly. So can assuming recent gains will continue indefinitely. Four years later, this bull market is still standing. For investors, the priority remains maintaining appropriate diversification, evaluating fundamentals and valuations, and aligning investment decisions with objectives, time horizons and risk tolerance within the context of each client’s broader total wealth plan.
